segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus and his disciples had also been invited to the wedding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have no wine.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, what do you want with me? My hour has not yet come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His mother said to the servants,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do whatever he tells you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now six stone water jars were standing there for the purification rites of the Jews, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Fill the jars with water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they filled them to the brim.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they took it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the master of the banquet tasted the water that had become wine—he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew—he called the bridegroom

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Everyone serves the good wine first, and the lesser wine once the guests are drunk. You have kept the good wine until now.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus did this, the beginning of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory, and his disciples trusted in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the temple he found those selling cattle and sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He made a whip out of cords and drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle; he poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To those selling the doves he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take these things out of here! Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples remembered that it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jewish leaders responded and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What sign do you show us, since you are doing these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Destroy this sanctuary, and in three days I will raise it up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the Jewish leaders said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This sanctuary took forty-six years to build, and you will raise it up in three days?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he was speaking about the sanctuary of his body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the festival, many trusted in his name, seeing the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, for his part, would not trust himself to them, because he knew everyone

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and had no need for anyone to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in a person.

notes.phrase: what do you want with me
notes.note: The Greek is a compressed idiom, literally “What to me and to you?” In the Greek Old Testament and elsewhere in the Gospels it is what someone says to keep another person at a distance, and it is rendered that way here. Some versions instead take it as “What concern is that to you and to me?”, making the shortage of wine the thing that concerns neither of them.

In Greek this was a courteous way to address a woman, with none of the harshness it has in English. Jesus uses it to other women and again to his mother from the cross (19:26). It is nonetheless a strikingly formal way for a son to speak to his mother, and English has no real equivalent.

The Greek says “two or three measures”; the measure in question held about ten gallons (roughly forty liters), so the six jars together held well over a hundred gallons. Stone jars were used for water for ritual washing because stone, unlike pottery, was regarded as not becoming ritually impure.

The Greek word is rare and names the person in charge of a banquet. It is uncertain whether this was a head servant who managed the meal or a guest chosen to preside over it. Older versions have “governor of the feast” or “ruler of the feast”; some recent ones have “chief steward.”

The verb means to become intoxicated, and many versions soften it to “have well drunk” or “have drunk freely.” The speaker is making a wry general remark about what hosts usually do, not describing the condition of the guests at this wedding.

The traditional rendering is “believed in him,” and the Greek verb covers both believing and trusting. “Trusted” is used here and in verse 23 because verse 24 plays on the same verb: many trusted in Jesus’s name, but he would not trust himself to them. In verse 22, where the object is the Scripture and Jesus’s saying, the same verb is rendered “believed.”

notes.phrase: both the sheep and the cattle
notes.note: The Greek can mean that Jesus drove out all the sellers together with their sheep and cattle, or that “all” refers only to the animals, which the phrase “both the sheep and the cattle” then spells out. The grammar does not settle it, and the rendering leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

notes.phrase: Zeal for your house will consume me
notes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9, the prayer of a righteous sufferer. The Hebrew psalm has a past tense (“has consumed me”); the future tense here is often taken to point ahead to Jesus’s death, though that is an inference.

The Greek says “the Jews.” Here, and in verse 20, those who challenge Jesus’s right to act in the temple are most naturally its authorities and not the Jewish people as a whole, to whom Jesus and his disciples themselves belonged. Scholars are divided on how to render the term in John: some argue for “Judeans” throughout, while others keep “the Jews” everywhere.

Most English versions use “temple” both for the word here and for the different word in verses 14–15. The word in verses 14–15 names the whole complex with its courts; this one names the sanctuary building itself, the place where God dwells, which is why Jesus can apply it to his body. Standard lexicons recognize the distinction, though scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers keep it.

The Greek verb is a simple past, which most naturally describes finished building, yet the rebuilding of the temple complex begun under Herod the Great was still in progress in Jesus’s day. Many versions therefore render “has been under construction for forty-six years.” The past tense is kept here; it may refer to a completed stage of the work or sum up the building to date.

candidates.reason: It needs to be fixed as “temple” (the whole complex) so that it never shares an English word with ναός, which the register renders “sanctuary.”

The choice between “raise” and “rise,” and between passive “was raised” and intransitive “rose,” recurs in every resurrection passage, and the sanctuary saying depends on one word covering both building and resurrection.
John’s theme of Jesus’s “hour” runs through the whole Gospel and would be obscured if some chapters rendered it “time.”
It is very frequent across the Gospels and Acts, and a translation with this stance could plausibly choose “student” or “follower,” so one decision is needed.

candidates.rendering: what do you want with me
candidates.reason: This idiom recurs in the Synoptics on the lips of demons (e.g. Mark 1:24, 5:7) and should be rendered in a recognizably uniform way.
